title: Neurodevelopment among children under five years with sickle cell disease in Eastern Uganda: A propensity score analysis
content:
by Bernard Maumbe, David Mukunya, Brendah Nambozo, Faith Oguttu, Julian Abeso, Sarah Mutonyi, Joel Okwir, Milton W. Musaba, Susan Lunyolo, Henry K. Nabudere, Lawrence Ssegawa, Deogratias Munube, Sarah Kiguli, Peter Olupot-Olupot

Aim

We compared neurodevelopment among children under-five years with and without sickle cell disease in eastern Uganda.

Methods

We conducted a cross-sectional study between March and September 2025 at the pediatric sickle cell clinic of Mbale Regional Referral Hospital. We included 350 children under five years (117 with sickle cell disease and 233 without sickle cell disease). The primary outcome was neurodevelopment assessed using the Malawi Development Assessment Tool. We performed independent sample t-tests to compare development for age z-scores between children with and without sickle cell disease. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses to calculate the effect of sickle cell disease on neurodevelopment.

Results

The median age of the children was 40.9 months (interquartile range 27.8 to 54.3 months). Children with sickle cell disease had 0.89 lower DAZ scores compared to their peers without sickle cell disease. Among the children with sickle cell disease, those not enrolled on hydroxyurea had 0.4 lower DAZ scores in the social and language domains compared to those on hydroxyurea. The average exposure effect, obtained from the inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses, was −0.87, 95% CI [−1.19, −0.55] and the average exposure effect among the exposed was – 0.62 95% CI [- 1.01, – 0.23].

Conclusion

Children with sickle cell disease had lower developmental scores across all domains (social, gross motor, fine motor and language) compared to community controls. These findings highlight the developmental vulnerability associated with sickle cell disease in early childhood. Efforts towards timely screening and management of developmental delays among children are needed to improve their quality of life and long-term development. This may be through integration of neurodevelopmental screening into routine sickle cell disease care.
author: Bernard Maumbe
